facts.statement: The subterranean city was accidentally rediscovered in 1963 when a local resident knocked through a basement wall during home renovations.

evidence.quote: Knowledge of the city faded until 1963, when it was rediscovered after a resident of the area, while renovating his home, knocked through a basement wall and found a mysterious room behind it.

facts.statement: The underground complex burrows to a depth of approximately 85 metres below the surface.

evidence.quote: Derinkuyu (Turkish pronunciation: [deˈɾinkuju]), also known as Malakopi, is an ancient multi-level underground city near the modern town of Derinkuyu in Nevşehir Province, Turkey, extending to a depth of approximately 85 metres (280 ft).
The ancient city of Elengubu, known today as Derinkuyu, burrows more than 85m below the Earth's surface, encompassing 18 levels of tunnels.
Derinkuyu Underground City The Derinkuyu Underground City has an approximate depth of 85 metres.

facts.statement: The subterranean city encompasses 18 levels of tunnels.

facts.statement: The complex was capable of sheltering up to 20,000 people alongside their livestock and food supplies.

evidence.quote: It is large enough to have sheltered as many as 20,000 people together with their livestock and food stores.

facts.statement: The entire city was hand-hewn directly out of tuff, a pliable rock composed of compacted volcanic ash.

evidence.quote: The underground city at Derinkuyu was carved mostly into tuff, a rock formed from compacted volcanic ash which is widespread in the region.

By Jennifer Pinkowski Published March 26, 2015 • 5 min read When the invaders came, Cappadocians knew where to hide: underground, in one of the 250 subterranean safe havens they had carved from pliable volcanic ash rock called tuff.

facts.statement: The earliest tunnels and chambers may date back to the 8th to 7th century BC, likely carved by the Phrygians.

evidence.quote: Tunnels and rooms might initially have been cut into the soft volcanic rock of the Cappadocia region by the Phrygians, in the 8th-7th century BC.
The largest excavated underground city in the world, it was in near-constant use for thousands of years, changing hands from the Phrygians to the Persians to the Christians of the Byzantine Era.
Derinkuyu’s origins may date back to around the eighth century B.C., with successive civilizations expanding it through at least the Byzantine era .

facts.statement: Derinkuyu was fully formed in the Byzantine era and substantially expanded during the Arab–Byzantine wars from roughly 780 to 1180 to protect local Christians.

evidence.quote: The city at Derinkuyu was fully formed in the Byzantine era.
The city was significantly enlarged during the Arab–Byzantine wars from roughly 780 to 1180, when it sheltered the local Christians from Umayyad and later Abbasid raider armies.

facts.statement: A central vertical ventilation shaft plunging 55 metres doubled as a water well serving both the subterranean inhabitants and the village above.

evidence.quote: The complex possesses a large amount of vertical ventilation shafts, divided into the smaller air vents that link living quarters and other individual rooms, to the wider central shafts, of which a 55-metre (180 ft) one appears to have been used as a well, providing water to both the villagers above and, if the outside world was not accessible, to those in hiding.
The ventilation shaft, which is 55 metres deep and connected to the surface, is also used as a water well.

facts.statement: The main ventilation shaft, measuring roughly 3 by 2.8 metres, was engineered so that openings on different subterranean levels never overlap, maximizing internal airflow.

evidence.quote: The main central shaft which measures roughly 3 m by 2.8 m and connects to several levels, never has the openings of two different levels overlapping one another, in a layout that appears deliberately engineered to maximise airflow.

facts.statement: Located on the second floor of the complex is a spacious room distinguished by a barrel-vaulted ceiling.

evidence.quote: Unique to the Derinkuyu complex is a spacious room with a barrel-vaulted ceiling located on the second floor.

facts.statement: The subterranean settlement was engineered with dedicated stables, cellars, refectories, wineries, oil presses, and chapels.

evidence.quote: The city could accommodate up to 20,000 people and had amenities found in other underground complexes across Cappadocia, such as wine and oil presses, stables, cellars, storage rooms, refectories, and chapels.
Excavation began immediately, revealing a tangled network of underground dwellings, dry food storage, cattle stables, schools, wineries and even a chapel.
The result is a vast underground complex with rooms, stables, cellars, tombs, schools and even churches with refectories.

facts.statement: The architectural layout allowed individual subterranean sections to be sealed off, enabling organized counterattacks if outer defenses were breached.

evidence.quote: The site's defensive underground design permitted not only concealment but the isolation of individual sections, internal movement of inhabitants, and even organised counterattacks if part of the city was breached.

facts.statement: Derinkuyu was linked to the neighboring underground city of Kaymakli across 8 to 9 kilometres of connecting tunnels.

facts.statement: Archaeologists have identified more than 600 separate entrances leading into the subterranean network, many hidden in private home basements.

evidence.quote: More than 600 separate tunnel entrances to the complex have since been discovered, some concealed under the basements of private houses in the above town.
It was the first of more than 600 entrances found within private homes leading to the subterrestrial city of Derinkuyu.

facts.statement: The underground complex was continuously used for shelter until it was completely abandoned following the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey.

evidence.quote: In the 20th century, the underground cities were still used by Cappadocian Greeks and Armenians to escape periodic persecutions.
In 1923, the Christian inhabitants of the region were expelled from Turkey and moved to Greece in the population exchange between Greece and Turkey, whereupon the underground city was abandoned.
It was finally abandoned in the 1920s by the Cappadocian Greeks when they faced defeat during the Greco-Turkish war and fled abruptly en masse to Greece.
